passage:
Subject: Can I meet you this week?
Dear Noor Ma'am,
I'm Manoj from 10C. You said in assembly that we could write to you if something was taking over our days. I think this is.
I keep scrolling through photos of people with perfect arms and flat stomachs. I know most of them are filtered, but I still compare myself. I've covered the mirror in my room with a poster. Last Sunday I pretended to have a stomach-ache so I wouldn't have to go to my cousin's engagement, because everyone takes photos. In class I'm thinking about how I look instead of the lesson. It feels like if I looked different I'd matter more.
My friends say everyone feels like this sometimes. Maybe. But for me it's all day now.
Could I come and see you after lunch on Wednesday?
Manoj

qa.q: What did Manoj cover the mirror with?
qa.a: A poster.

qa.q: What does Manoj think would change if Manoj looked different?
qa.a: Manoj feels insecure and thinks a different look would make Manoj matter more, tying worth to appearance.

qa.q: Why was writing this email a turning point for Manoj?
qa.a: Manoj noticed the thoughts had spread to the whole day, not just sometimes, and chose to ask the counsellor for help early.

qa.q: How might Noor Ma'am feel reading "for me it's all day now"?
qa.a: Noor Ma'am may be glad Manoj wrote and take it seriously, since it shows the worry has grown beyond the ordinary.

grounding: It shows a teenager comparing themselves to filtered photos, avoiding mirrors and gatherings and tying worth to looks, then seeking help when the thoughts fill the day.

passage: Thanks for having me on the youth show, Urmila. So, last year I quit swimming. Not because I stopped loving it. Because of the changing room. I'd spent nights comparing myself to people online, all shiny and edited, and in my head I was the wrong shape. I stopped going to family dinners because someone always says, "You've grown." I'd take three selfies, edit my face, and still hate them. It got to where every thought was about my body: in maths, at the bus stop, before sleep. One day Coach asked why I'd stopped coming, and I just said it. He didn't laugh. He said lots of people feel this way, but if it's filling the whole day, a doctor or counsellor should know. My mum took me that week. I'm Abhinav, by the way, and I'm back in the pool now. Some days.

qa.q: Why did Abhinav quit swimming?
qa.a: Because of the changing room.

qa.q: How did Abhinav feel about the selfies even after editing them?
qa.a: Abhinav still hated them and felt insecure about being 'the wrong shape', a harsh view that no editing could fix.

qa.q: What choice changed things for Abhinav, and what followed?
qa.a: Abhinav told Coach the real reason; Coach said a doctor or counsellor should know, and Mum took Abhinav that week.

qa.q: How might Coach have seen Abhinav's absence before that day?
qa.a: He may have thought Abhinav had lost interest, and learned only by asking that a painful body worry was keeping Abhinav away.

grounding: It shows a teenager comparing their body to edited images, avoiding the pool and family dinners, and getting help once the thoughts filled every part of the day.

passage:
PE teacher's note, Class 10, Friday.
Kashish, fifteen, has missed swimming four weeks in a row with different excuses. In the dance room she stands at the back, turned away from the mirrors. Today I saw her scrolling through filtered photos of influencers, then she whispered to a friend, "I look disgusting next to them." She has also skipped the class picnic and the annual photo.
After class I asked if she was all right. She said she thinks about how she looks "every minute of the day" and it makes it hard to study. I told her many teenagers feel badly about their bodies, and that when it takes over the whole day, it's time to get help. With her agreement, I walked her to the school counsellor and we informed her parents. — Thomas

qa.q: How many weeks in a row has Kashish missed swimming?
qa.a: Four weeks in a row.

qa.q: How does Kashish feel about her body?
qa.a: She feels ashamed and disgusted, comparing herself to filtered photos and thinking about her looks every minute.

qa.q: What did Thomas do that was wise?
qa.a: Thomas asked privately, reassured Kashish that such feelings are common, and because the thoughts were taking over the day, walked her to the counsellor and informed her parents.

qa.q: How might Kashish's friend have felt hearing her whisper?
qa.a: The friend may have felt surprised and worried, not realising Kashish saw herself so harshly.

grounding: Shows a teenager who compares herself to filtered images, avoids mirrors and gatherings and links worth to looks, and a teacher who helps her seek support.

passage:
Sunday
Didn't go to Eshaan's birthday party. Told Ammi I had a headache. The truth is there'd be photos, and I can't stand seeing myself in photos next to my cousins.
I spent two hours looking at pictures online of girls with perfect skin and tiny waists. I know they're filtered. I KNOW. But I still felt ugly.
I put my dupatta over the mirror in my room. Every thought today was about my face, my arms, my stomach. I couldn't even finish my chemistry.
I think this is getting too big. Ammi came to check on me and I almost told her. Tomorrow I'll tell her properly, and ask to see the school counsellor.
Rehana

qa.q: What did Rehana put over the mirror?
qa.a: Rehana put a dupatta over the mirror.

qa.q: How did Rehana feel after looking at pictures online?
qa.a: Rehana felt ugly and ashamed, even knowing the pictures were filtered.

qa.q: What is Rehana planning to do, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Rehana plans to tell Ammi properly and ask for the school counsellor, because the thoughts are taking over the whole day.

qa.q: How might Eshaan feel about Rehana missing the party?
qa.a: Eshaan may feel disappointed, not knowing the real reason was fear of being in photos.

grounding: Shows a teenager comparing their looks with filtered images, avoiding mirrors and a gathering, linking worth to looks, and deciding to seek help as it takes over.

passage:
In the small town of Nanded, Hemant, fifteen, spent his evenings scrolling through photos of gym boys online, every one of them smooth and perfect. He knew some were edited. It didn't help.
He stopped taking his shirt off at the river with friends. He turned the bathroom mirror slightly so he couldn't see himself. When his cousin's wedding came, he told his mother he had a stomach ache and stayed home.
"If I looked different, people would actually like me," he wrote in his notebook.
His sister Parul found him in the dark with his phone, still scrolling at midnight. "You didn't come to the wedding. You don't go to the river. Is this about how you look?"
Hemant said nothing for a long time. Then, "I can't stop thinking about it. All day."
"Then let's tell someone who knows how to help," Parul said. The next morning they went to the school counsellor together.

qa.q: What did Hemant do to the bathroom mirror?
qa.a: He turned it slightly so he couldn't see himself.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling when he wrote in his notebook?
qa.a: He felt worthless and insecure, believing people would only like him if he looked different.

qa.q: Why was it right for Hemant to seek help?
qa.a: Because the thoughts about his body were taking over his whole day and making him avoid friends and family events, not just ordinary bad feelings.

qa.q: How does Parul see her brother's change?
qa.a: Parul notices his missed wedding and river trips, feels worried, and cares enough to gently ask and go with him for help.

grounding: Hemant compares himself to edited images, avoids mirrors and gatherings and links worth to looks, and seeks help when the thoughts take over his day.
